shortness-of-life_section-01.originalText:
The greater part of mankind, my Paulinus, complains of the
unkindness of Nature, because we are born only for a short space
of time, and that this allotted period of life runs away so swiftly,
nay so hurriedly, that with but few exceptions men’s life comes to
an end just as they are preparing to enjoy it: nor is it only the
common herd and the ignorant vulgar who mourn over this universal
misfortune, as they consider it to be: this reflection has wrung
complaints even from great men. Hence comes that well-known saying
of physicians, that art is long but life is short: hence arose that
quarrel, so unbefitting a sage, which Aristotle picked with Nature,
because she had indulged animals with such length of days that some
of them lived for ten or fifteen centuries, while man, although
born for many and such great exploits, had the term of his existence
cut so much shorter.
shortness-of-life_section-01.plainEnglish: Most people, Paulinus, complain that nature has been unfair to us. They say we are born with too little time, and that even the time we are given slips away far too quickly — so fast that most men die just as they're getting ready to really live. It's not just ordinary people and the ignorant masses who feel this way. Even great men have complained about what they see as this universal misfortune. That's where the famous medical saying comes from: "Art is long, but life is short." That's also why Aristotle — who should have known better — picked a foolish fight with Nature. He was angry that she gave animals such long lives that some live for ten or fifteen centuries, while humans, who are born for so many great achievements, get their lives cut so much shorter.

shortness-of-life_section-01.originalText:
We do not have a very short time assigned to
us, but we lose a great deal of it: life is long enough to carry
out the most important projects: we have an ample portion,
if we do but arrange the whole of it aright: but when it all runs
to waste through luxury and carelessness, when it is not devoted
to any good purpose, then at the last we are forced to feel that
it is all over, although we never noticed how it glided away. Thus
it is: we do not receive a short life, but we make it a short one,
and we are not poor in days, but wasteful of them. When great and
kinglike riches fall into the hands of a bad master, they are
dispersed straightway, but even a moderate fortune, when bestowed
upon a wise guardian, increases by use: and in like manner our life
has great opportunities for one who knows how to dispose of it to
the best advantage.
shortness-of-life_section-01.plainEnglish: We haven't been given a short life. We've just wasted a lot of it. Life is long enough to do great things — if you stop throwing it away. We have plenty of time if we use it wisely. But when we waste it on luxury and carelessness, when we don't put it toward anything worthwhile, then suddenly we feel like it's all over. We never even noticed how it slipped away. Here's the truth: we don't receive a short life, but we make it short. We're not poor in days — we're wasteful with them. When great wealth falls into the hands of a bad owner, it disappears right away. But even a modest fortune grows when a wise person manages it. Our life works the same way. It offers great opportunities to anyone who knows how to use it well.

shortness-of-life_section-02.originalText: Why do we complain of Nature? she has dealt kindly with us. Life is long enough, if you know how to use it. One man is possessed by an avarice which nothing can satisfy, another by a laborious diligence in doing what is totally useless: another is sodden by wine: another is benumbed by sloth: one man is exhausted by an ambition which makes him court the good will of others: another, through his eagerness as a merchant, is led to visit every land and every sea by the hope of gain: some are plagued by the love of soldiering, and are always either endangering other men's lives or in trembling for their own: some wear away their lives in that voluntary slavery, the unrequited service of great men: many are occupied either in laying claim to other men's fortune or in complaining of their own: a great number have no settled purpose, and are tossed from one new scheme to another by a rambling, inconsistent, dissatisfied, fickle habit of mind: some care for no object sufficiently to try to attain it, but lie lazily yawning until their fate comes upon them: so that I cannot doubt the truth of that verse which the greatest of poets has dressed in the guise of an oracular response—"We live a small part only of our lives."
shortness-of-life_section-02.plainEnglish: Why do we complain about nature? She has been kind to us. Life is long enough — if you know how to use it. One man is consumed by greed that nothing can satisfy. Another works himself to death on completely useless tasks. Another drowns himself in wine. Another is paralyzed by laziness. One man exhausts himself with ambition, always trying to win other people's approval. Another travels to every land and sea, chasing profits as a merchant. Some are obsessed with war, constantly putting other lives in danger or fearing for their own. Others waste their lives as voluntary slaves, serving powerful men who give nothing back. Many spend their time either scheming to steal other people's fortunes or complaining about their own. A great number have no clear purpose at all. They drift from one half-baked plan to another, restless and fickle and never satisfied. Some care so little about anything that they don't even try to achieve it — they just lie around yawning until death comes for them. So I have no doubt that the greatest poet was right when he wrote these words like a prophecy: 'We live only a small part of our lives.'

shortness-of-life_section-02.originalText: But all duration is time, not life: vices press upon us and surround us on every side, and do not permit us to regain our feet, or to raise our eyes and gaze upon truth, but when we are down keep us prostrate and chained to low desires. Men who are in this condition are never allowed to come to themselves: if ever by chance they obtain any rest, they roll to and fro like the deep sea, which heaves and tosses after a gale, and they never have any respite from their lusts. Do you suppose that I speak of those whose ills are notorious? Nay, look at those whose prosperity all men run to see: they are choked by their own good things. To how many men do riches prove a heavy burden? how many men's eloquence and continual desire to display their own cleverness has cost them their lives? how many are sallow with constant sensual indulgence? how many have no freedom left them by the tribe of clients that surges around them?
shortness-of-life_section-02.plainEnglish: But having time is not the same as living. Vices attack us from all sides and keep us trapped. They don't let us get back on our feet or look up to see the truth. Instead, they keep us flat on the ground, chained to shallow desires. People caught in this trap never get a chance to recover. Even when they get a brief break, they roll around like the ocean after a storm — never getting real rest from their cravings. You think I'm only talking about people whose problems are obvious? No, look at those everyone envies for their success. They're suffocating under their own good fortune. How many people are crushed by their wealth? How many have died because of their eloquence and constant need to show off how clever they are? How many have grown pale from endless indulgence? How many have lost all freedom because of the crowds of hangers-on who swarm around them?

shortness-of-life_section-02.originalText: Look through all these, from the lowest to the highest:—this man calls his friends to support him, this one is present in court, this one is the defendant, this one pleads for him, this one is on the jury: but no one lays claim to his own self, every one wastes his time over some one else. Investigate those men, whose names are in every one's mouth: you will find that they bear just the same marks: A is devoted to B, and B to C: no one belongs to himself. Moreover some men are full of most irrational anger: they complain of the insolence of their chiefs, because they have not granted them an audience when they wished for it; as if a man had any right to complain of being so haughtily shut out by another, when he never has leisure to give his own conscience a hearing. This chief of yours, whoever he is, though he may look at you in an offensive manner, still will some day look at you, open his ears to your words, and give you a seat by his side: but you never design to look upon yourself, to listen to your own grievances. You ought not, then, to claim these services from another, especially since while you yourself were doing so, you did not wish for an interview with another man, but were not able to obtain one with yourself.
shortness-of-life_section-02.plainEnglish: Look at everyone around you, from the lowest to the highest. This man calls his friends to help him. That one shows up in court. Another one is the defendant. This one argues his case. That one sits on the jury. But no one claims time for himself. Everyone wastes their time on someone else. Look at those famous people whose names everyone knows. You'll see they have the same problem. Person A devotes himself to Person B, and Person B to Person C. No one belongs to himself. Some people get irrationally angry. They complain that their bosses are arrogant because they won't grant them a meeting when they want one. But how can you complain about someone shutting you out when you never give yourself time to listen to your own conscience? Your boss, whoever he is, may look at you rudely now, but someday he will look at you, listen to your words, and give you a seat next to him. But you never bother to look at yourself or listen to your own complaints. So you shouldn't demand these services from others — especially since when you were doing all this running around, you didn't want a meeting with another person. You just couldn't get one with yourself.

shortness-of-life_section-03.originalText: Were all the brightest intellects of all time to employ themselves on this one subject, they never could sufficiently express their wonder at this blindness of men's minds: men will not allow any one to establish himself upon their estates, and upon the most trifling dispute about the measuring of boundaries, they betake themselves to stones and cudgels: yet they allow others to encroach upon their lives, nay, they themselves actually lead others in to take possession of them. You cannot find any one who wants to distribute his money; yet among how many people does every one distribute his life? men covetously guard their property from waste, but when it comes to waste of time, they are most prodigal of that of which it would become them to be sparing.
shortness-of-life_section-03.plainEnglish: Even if all the greatest minds in history worked together on this problem, they could never fully capture how blind we are about this. People won't let anyone set up shop on their land. They'll grab rocks and clubs over the tiniest property line dispute. Yet they let others invade their lives — worse, they actually invite people in to take over. You can't find anyone willing to give away their money. But everyone gives away their time to countless people. We jealously protect our possessions from waste. But when it comes to wasting time — the one thing we should guard most carefully — we throw it around like it's worthless.

shortness-of-life_section-03.originalText: Let us take one of the elders, and say to him, "We perceive that you have arrived at the extreme limits of human life: you are in your hundredth year, or even older. Come now, reckon up your whole life in black and white: tell us how much of your time has been spent upon your creditors, how much on your mistress, how much on your king, how much on your clients, how much in quarrelling with your wife, how much in keeping your slaves in order, how much in running up and down the city on business. Add to this the diseases which we bring upon us with our own hands, and the time which has laid idle without any use having been made of it; you will see that you have not lived as many years as you count. Look back in your memory and see how often you have been consistent in your projects, how many days passed as you intended them to do when you were at your own disposal, how often you did not change colour and your spirit did not quail, how much work you have done in so long a time, how many people have without your knowledge stolen parts of your life from you, how much you have lost, how large a part has been taken up by useless grief, foolish gladness, greedy desire, or polite conversation; how little of yourself is left to you: you will then perceive that you will die prematurely."
shortness-of-life_section-03.plainEnglish: Let's take one of these old people and ask him: "We see you've reached the very end of human life. You're a hundred years old, maybe more. Now sit down and add up your whole life like a ledger. Tell us how much time you spent on your creditors, how much on your lover, how much serving your king, how much on your clients, how much fighting with your wife, how much managing your slaves, how much running around the city on business. Add in the illnesses you brought on yourself and all the time that just sat there unused. You'll see that you haven't actually lived as many years as you think you have. Look back and remember: how often did you stick to your plans? How many days went exactly as you wanted when you were free to choose? How often did you not turn pale with fear or lose your nerve? What did you actually accomplish in all that time? How many people stole pieces of your life without you even noticing? How much did you lose? How much was eaten up by pointless grief, empty pleasures, desperate wanting, or small talk? How little of yourself is actually left? Then you'll realize you're dying too early."

shortness-of-life_section-03.originalText: What, then, is the reason of this? It is that people live as though they would live for ever: you never remember your human frailty; you never notice how much of your time has already gone by: you spend it as though you had an abundant and overflowing store of it, though all the while that day which you devote to some man or to some thing is perhaps your last. You fear everything, like mortals as you are, and yet you desire everything as if you were immortals.
shortness-of-life_section-03.plainEnglish: So what's the problem? People live as if they'll never die. You forget how fragile you are. You don't notice how much time has already slipped away. You spend time carelessly, as if you have endless supplies of it. But that day you're wasting on someone or something might be your last. You fear everything like the mortal you are, yet you want everything as if you'll live forever.

shortness-of-life_section-03.originalText: You will hear many men say, "After my fiftieth year I will give myself up to leisure: my sixtieth shall be my last year of public office": and what guarantee have you that your life will last any longer? who will let all this go on just as you have arranged it? are you not ashamed to reserve only the leavings of your life for yourself, and appoint for the enjoyment of your own right mind only that time which you cannot devote to any business? How late it is to begin life just when we have to be leaving it! What a foolish forgetfulness of our mortality, to put off wholesome counsels until our fiftieth or sixtieth year, and to choose that our lives shall begin at a point which few of us ever reach.
shortness-of-life_section-03.plainEnglish: You'll hear many men say, "After I turn fifty, I'll finally take time for myself. When I'm sixty, I'll retire from public life." But what guarantee do you have that you'll live that long? Who says everything will go according to your plan? Aren't you ashamed to save only the scraps of your life for yourself? You're planning to enjoy your own peace of mind only when you can't do anything else anymore. How ridiculous to start living just when you have to die! What foolish forgetfulness of death — to put off wise decisions until your fifties or sixties. You're choosing to begin your life at an age that most people never even reach.

shortness-of-life_section-04.originalText: You will find that the most powerful and highly-placed men let fall phrases in which they long for leisure, praise it, and prefer it to all the blessings which they enjoy. Sometimes they would fain descend from their lofty pedestal, if it could be safely done: for Fortune collapses by its own weight, without any shock or interference from without.
shortness-of-life_section-04.plainEnglish: You'll notice that the most powerful and high-ranking men often say things that show they crave free time. They praise it and would choose it over all the privileges they currently enjoy. Sometimes they wish they could step down from their high positions — if only they could do it safely. But fortune has a way of collapsing under its own weight, even without any outside push or interference.

shortness-of-life_section-04.originalText: The late Emperor Augustus, upon whom the gods bestowed more blessings than on any one else, never ceased to pray for rest and exemption from the troubles of empire: he used to enliven his labours with this sweet, though unreal consolation, that he would some day live for himself alone. In a letter which he addressed to the Senate, after promising that his rest shall not be devoid of dignity nor discreditable to his former glories, I find the following words:—"These things, however, it is more honourable to do than to promise: but my eagerness for that time, so earnestly longed for, has led me to derive a certain pleasure from speaking about it, though the reality is still far distant." He thought leisure so important, that though he could not actually enjoy it, yet he did so by anticipation and by thinking about it.
shortness-of-life_section-04.plainEnglish: Even the late Emperor Augustus — who received more blessings from the gods than anyone else — never stopped wishing for rest. He wanted to escape the constant troubles of running the empire. He used to comfort himself with one sweet thought (though it was just a dream): someday he would live for himself alone. In a letter to the Senate, he promised that his retirement would be dignified and worthy of his past achievements. Then he wrote these words: "Of course, it's better to actually do these things than just promise them. But I'm so eager for that time I've been longing for that I get real pleasure just from talking about it, even though it's still far away." Augustus thought leisure was so valuable that even though he couldn't have it, he enjoyed it by imagining it and planning for it.

shortness-of-life_section-04.originalText: He, who saw everything depending upon himself alone, who swayed the fortunes of men and of nations, thought that his happiest day would be that on which he laid aside his greatness. He knew by experience how much labour was involved in that glory that shone through all lands, and how much secret anxiety was concealed within it: he had been forced to assert his rights by war, first with his countrymen, next with his colleagues, and lastly with his own relations, and had shed blood both by sea and by land: after marching his troops under arms through Macedonia, Sicily, Egypt, Syria, Asia Minor, and almost all the countries of the world, when they were weary with slaughtering Romans he had directed them against a foreign foe.
shortness-of-life_section-04.plainEnglish: He saw that everything depended on him alone. He controlled the fate of individuals and entire nations. Yet he believed his happiest day would be when he gave up all that power. He knew from experience how much work went into that glory that reached every corner of the world. He knew how much hidden worry it contained. He had been forced to fight wars to protect his position — first against his own countrymen, then against his allies, and finally against his own family. He had spilled blood on both sea and land. He had marched his armies through Macedonia, Sicily, Egypt, Syria, Asia Minor, and almost every country in the world. When his troops grew tired of killing Romans, he turned them against foreign enemies instead.

shortness-of-life_section-04.originalText: While he was pacifying the Alpine regions, and subduing the enemies whom he found in the midst of the Roman empire, while he was extending its boundaries beyond the Rhine, the Euphrates, and the Danube, at Rome itself the swords of Murena, Caepio, Lepidus, Egnatius, and others were being sharpened to slay him. Scarcely had he escaped from their plot, when his already failing age was terrified by his daughter and all the noble youths who were pledged to her cause by adultery with her by way of oath of fidelity. Then there was Paulus and Antonius's mistress, a second time to be feared by Rome: and when he had cut out these ulcers from his very limbs, others grew in their place: the empire, like a body overloaded with blood, was always breaking out somewhere. For this reason he longed for leisure: all his labours were based upon hopes and thoughts of leisure: this was the wish of him who could accomplish the wishes of all other men.
shortness-of-life_section-04.plainEnglish: While Augustus was conquering the Alpine regions and defeating enemies within the Roman empire, while he was pushing the borders beyond the Rhine, Euphrates, and Danube rivers, back in Rome itself the swords of Murena, Caepio, Lepidus, Egnatius, and others were being sharpened to kill him. He had barely escaped their plot when his failing health was shaken by his daughter's scandal and all the noble young men who had sworn loyalty to her through adultery. Then came the threat of Paulus and Antony's mistress — a second danger to Rome. When he had cut out these cancers from his own body, new ones grew in their place. The empire was like a body with too much blood — always bursting out somewhere. This is why he longed for peace and quiet. All his work was built on hopes of eventual rest. This was the one wish of the man who could grant everyone else's wishes.

shortness-of-life_section-05.originalText:
While tossed hither and thither by Catiline and Clodius, Pompeius
and Crassus, by some open enemies and some doubtful friends, while
he struggled with the struggling republic and kept it from going
to ruin, when at last he was banished, being neither able to keep
silence in prosperity nor to endure adversity with patience, how
often must Marcus Cicero have cursed that consulship of his which
he never ceased to praise, and which nevertheless deserved it? What
piteous expressions he uses in a letter to Atticus when Pompeius
the father had been defeated, and his son was recruiting his shattered
forces in Spain? “Do you ask,” writes he, “what I am doing here? I
am living in my Tusculan villa almost as a prisoner.” He adds more
afterwards, wherein he laments his former life, complains of the
present, and despairs of the future. Cicero called himself “half a
prisoner,” but, by Hercules, the wise man never would have come
under so lowly a title: he never would be half a prisoner, but would
always enjoy complete and entire liberty, being free, in his own
power, and greater than all others: for what can be greater than
the man who is greater than Fortune?
shortness-of-life_section-05.plainEnglish: Look at Marcus Cicero's life. He was thrown around by Catiline and Clodius, by Pompey and Crassus — some open enemies, some unreliable friends. He fought to save the failing republic and keep it from collapse. But then he was exiled. He couldn't stay quiet when things went well, and he couldn't handle adversity with grace. How often he must have cursed that famous consulship of his — the one he never stopped bragging about, even though it did deserve praise! You can see his misery in a letter to Atticus, written after Pompey the elder was defeated and his son was trying to rebuild his broken forces in Spain. "Do you ask what I'm doing here?" Cicero writes. "I'm living in my villa near Tusculum, almost like a prisoner." He goes on to mourn his past life, complain about the present, and despair about the future. Cicero called himself "half a prisoner." But by god, a wise man would never accept such a lowly title. He would never be half a prisoner. He would always enjoy complete and total freedom — free, in control of himself, and greater than everyone else. For what can be greater than the man who is greater than Fortune?

shortness-of-life_section-06.originalText: When Livius Drusus, a vigorous and energetic man, brought forward bills for new laws and radical measures of the Gracchus pattern, being the centre of a vast mob of all the peoples of Italy, and seeing no way to solve the question, since he was not allowed to deal with it as he wished, and yet was not free to throw it up after having once taken part in it, complained bitterly of his life, which had been one of unrest from the very cradle, and said, we are told, that "he was the only person who had never had any holidays even when he was a boy." Indeed, while he was still under age and wearing the praetexta, he had the courage to plead the cause of accused persons in court, and to make use of his influence so powerfully that it is well known that in some causes his exertions gained a verdict. Where would such precocious ambition stop? You may be sure that one who showed such boldness as a child would end by becoming a great pest both in public and in private life: it was too late for him to complain that he had had no holidays, when from his boyhood he had been a firebrand and a nuisance in the courts. It is a stock question whether he committed suicide: for he fell by a sudden wound in the groin, and some doubted whether his death was caused by his own hand, though none disputed its having happened most seasonably.
shortness-of-life_section-06.plainEnglish: Take Livius Drusus — an energetic, ambitious man who pushed for new laws and radical reforms like the Gracchus brothers had. He found himself surrounded by massive crowds from all over Italy, but he couldn't see any way out of the mess he'd created. He wasn't allowed to handle things the way he wanted, but he also couldn't just walk away after getting so deep into it. So he complained bitterly about his life, saying it had been nothing but stress since he was born. He used to say that "he was the only person who never had any holidays, not even as a boy." Even as a child, still wearing his youth toga, he was bold enough to defend accused people in court. He used his influence so powerfully that everyone knew he could swing verdicts in some cases just by his efforts. Where would such early ambition lead? You can be sure that someone who showed such nerve as a child would grow up to be a major problem in both public and private life. It was too late for him to complain about never having holidays when he'd been stirring up trouble in the courts since boyhood. People still debate whether he killed himself. He died from a sudden wound to the groin, and some questioned whether it was by his own hand — though no one argued that his death came at exactly the right time.

shortness-of-life_section-06.originalText: It would be superfluous to mention more who, while others thought them the happiest of men, have themselves borne true witness to their own feelings, and have loathed all that they have done for all the years of their lives: yet by these complaints they have effected no alteration either in others or in themselves: for after these words have escaped them their feelings revert to their accustomed frame. By Hercules, that life of you great men, even though it should last for more than a thousand years, is still a very short one: those vices of yours would swallow up any extent of time: no wonder if this our ordinary span, which, though Nature hurries on, can be enlarged by common sense, soon slips away from you; for you do not lay hold of it or hold it back, and try to delay the swiftest of all things, but you let it pass as though it were a useless thing and you could supply its place.
shortness-of-life_section-06.plainEnglish: I could name many more examples, but it's pointless. These were men everyone else thought were incredibly happy. Yet they gave honest testimony about their own lives — they hated everything they had done for years. But their complaints changed nothing, not in others and not in themselves. After speaking these words, they went right back to their old habits. I swear, even if you powerful men lived for a thousand years, your lives would still be too short. Your vices would devour any amount of time you were given. No wonder our normal lifespan slips away from you so quickly. Yes, nature rushes time along, but common sense can stretch it. You don't grab hold of time or try to slow it down. You don't try to delay the fastest thing in existence. Instead, you let it pass by as if it were worthless — as if you could just replace it later.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Among these I reckon in the first place those who devote their time to nothing but drinking and debauchery: for no men are busied more shamefully: the others, although the glory which they pursue is but a counterfeit, still deserve some credit for their pursuit of it—though you may tell me of misers, of passionate men, of men who hate and who even wage war without a cause—yet all such men sin like men: but the sin of those who are given up to gluttony and lust is a disgraceful one. Examine all the hours of their lives: consider how much time they spend in calculation, how much in plotting, how much in fear, how much in giving and deceiving flattery, how much in entering into recognizances for themselves or for others, how much in banquets, which indeed become a serious business, you will see that they are not allowed any breathing time either by their pleasures or their pains.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: I think first of people who spend all their time drinking and living wildly. No one wastes their life more shamefully. Other people — even the greedy, the angry, the hateful, those who start pointless wars — at least chase after some kind of glory, even if it's fake. They sin, but they sin like human beings. But people who give themselves over to gluttony and lust? That's just disgraceful. Look at how they spend their hours. Count up the time they spend scheming, plotting, worrying, giving fake compliments, making deals for themselves and others, hosting dinner parties that become serious business. You'll see they get no rest — not from their pleasures, not from their troubles.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Finally, all are agreed that nothing, neither eloquence nor literature, can be done properly by one who is occupied with something else; for nothing can take deep root in a mind which is directed to some other subject, and which rejects whatever you try to stuff into it. No man knows less about living than a business man: there is nothing about which it is more difficult to gain knowledge. Other arts have many folk everywhere who profess to teach them: some of them can be so thoroughly learned by mere boys, that they are able to teach them to others: but one's whole life must be spent in learning how to live, and, which may perhaps surprise you more, one's whole life must be spent in learning how to die.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: Everyone agrees on this: you can't do anything well — whether it's speaking or writing — if you're distracted by other things. Nothing can grow deep roots in a mind that's pulled in different directions and rejects whatever you try to cram into it. No one knows less about living than a businessman. There's nothing harder to learn than how to live. Other skills have plenty of teachers everywhere. Some can be mastered so well by children that they can teach them to others. But learning how to live takes your entire lifetime. And what might surprise you even more — learning how to die also takes your entire lifetime.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Many excellent men have freed themselves from all hindrances, have given up riches, business, and pleasure, and have made it their duty to the very end of their lives to learn how to live: and yet the larger portion of them leave this life confessing that they do not yet know how to live, and still less know how to live as wise men. Believe me, it requires a great man and one who is superior to human frailties not to allow any of his time to be filched from him: and therefore it follows that his life is a very long one, because he devotes every possible part of it to himself: no portion lies idle or uncultivated, or in another man's power; for he finds nothing worthy of being exchanged for his time, which he husbands most grudgingly. He, therefore, had time enough: whereas those who gave up a great part of their lives to the people of necessity had not enough.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: Many excellent men have freed themselves from all distractions. They've given up wealth, business, and pleasure. They've made it their life's work to learn how to live well. Yet most of them die admitting they still don't know how to live — let alone how to live wisely. Believe me, it takes a great person, someone above ordinary human weaknesses, to stop others from stealing his time. That's why his life feels very long. He gives every possible moment to himself. No part of his time sits idle or wasted or under someone else's control. He finds nothing worth trading for his time, which he guards fiercely. So he has enough time. But those who gave most of their lives to other people? They never had enough.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Yet you need not suppose that the latter were not sometimes conscious of their loss: indeed, you will hear most of those who are troubled with great prosperity every now and then cry out amid their hosts of clients, their pleadings in court, and their other honourable troubles, "I am not allowed to live my own life." Why is he not allowed? because all those who call upon you to defend them, take you away from yourself. How many of your days have been spent by that defendant? by that candidate for office? by that old woman who is weary with burying her heirs? by that man who pretends to be ill, in order to excite the greed of those who hope to inherit his property? by that powerful friend of yours, who uses you to swell his train, not to be his friend? Balance your account, and run over all the days of your life; you will see that only a very few days, and only those which were useless for any other purpose, have been left to you.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: Don't think that successful people don't realize what they're losing. You'll often hear those blessed with great prosperity cry out — right in the middle of their crowded schedules, their court cases, and their other prestigious burdens — "I can't live my own life!" Why can't they? Because everyone who asks for their help pulls them away from themselves. How many of your days have been eaten up by that lawsuit? By that politician seeking office? By that old woman who's tired of burying her heirs? By that man who fakes illness to get people excited about his inheritance? By that powerful friend who uses you as decoration for his entourage, not as a real friend? Do the math. Go through all the days of your life. You'll see that only a few days are left for you — and those are usually the ones nobody else wanted anyway.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: He who has obtained the _fasces_ for which he longed, is eager to get rid of them, and is constantly saying, "When will this year be over?" another exhibits public games, and once would have given a great deal for the chance of doing so, but now "when," says he, "shall I escape from this?" another is an advocate who is fought for in all the courts, and who draws immense audiences, who crowd all the forum to a far greater distance than they can hear him; "When," says he, "will vacation-time come?" Every man hurries through his life, and suffers from a yearning for the future, and a weariness of the present: but he who disposes of all his time for his own purposes, who arranges all his days as though he were arranging the plan of his life, neither wishes for nor fears the morrow: for what new pleasure can any hour now bestow upon him? he knows it all, and has indulged in it all even to satiety.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: The man who finally gets the political office he craved now wants to escape it. He keeps saying, 'When will this year be over?' Another person puts on expensive public games — something he once would have paid anything to do. But now he asks, 'When can I get out of this?' A famous lawyer draws huge crowds that pack the entire forum far beyond where they can even hear him. Yet he asks, 'When does vacation start?' Everyone rushes through life. They long for the future and feel tired of the present. But the person who uses all his time for his own purposes — who plans each day like he's planning his whole life — doesn't wish for tomorrow or fear it. What new pleasure could any hour give him? He knows them all and has enjoyed them to the point of being sick of them.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Fortune may deal with the rest as she will, his life is already safe from her: such a man may gain something, but cannot lose anything: and, indeed, he can only gain anything in the same way as one who is already glutted and filled can get some extra food which he takes although he does not want it. You have no grounds, therefore, for supposing that any one has lived long, because he has wrinkles or grey hairs: such a man has not lived long, but has only been long alive. Why! would you think that a man had voyaged much if a fierce gale had caught him as soon as he left his port, and he had been driven round and round the same place continually by a succession of winds blowing from opposite quarters? such a man has not travelled much, he has only been much tossed about.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: Fortune can do what she wants with everything else — his life is already protected from her. A man like this might gain something, but he can't lose anything. He can only gain more the way someone who's already stuffed can take extra food he doesn't even want. So don't assume someone has lived long just because he has wrinkles or gray hair. That person hasn't lived long — he's just been alive for a long time. Would you say a sailor had traveled far if a storm caught him right after leaving port and blew him in circles with winds from every direction? That man didn't travel much. He just got tossed around a lot.

shortness-of-life_section-08.originalText: I am filled with wonder when I see some men asking others for their time, and those who are asked for it most willing to give it: both parties consider the object for which the time is given, but neither of them thinks of the time itself, as though in asking for this one asked for nothing, and in giving it one gave nothing: we play with what is the most precious of all things: yet it escapes men's notice, because it is an incorporeal thing, and because it does not come before our eyes; and therefore it is held very cheap, nay, hardly any value whatever is put upon it. Men set the greatest store upon presents or pensions, and hire out their work, their services, or their care in order to gain them: no one values time: they give it much more freely, as though it cost nothing.
shortness-of-life_section-08.plainEnglish: I'm amazed when I see people asking others for their time, and how willingly they give it. Both sides think about what the time will be used for, but neither thinks about the time itself. It's as if asking for time costs nothing and giving it away is free. We waste the most precious thing we have. People don't notice this because time isn't something you can touch or see. So we treat it as worthless — or nearly worthless. People treasure gifts and money. They work hard for wages and benefits. But no one values time. They give it away freely, as if it costs nothing.

shortness-of-life_section-08.originalText: Yet you will see these same people clasping the knees of their physician as suppliants when they are sick and in present peril of death, and if threatened with a capital charge willing to give all that they possess in order that they may live: so inconsistent are they. Indeed, if the number of every man's future years could be laid before him, as we can lay that of his past years, how anxious those who found that they had but few years remaining would be to make the most of them? Yet it is easy to arrange the distribution of a quantity, however small, if we know how much there is: what you ought to husband most carefully is that which may run short you know not when.
shortness-of-life_section-08.plainEnglish: Yet you'll see these same people begging their doctor on their knees when they're sick and facing death. If charged with a crime that could kill them, they'd give away everything they own just to stay alive. How contradictory they are! If we could see exactly how many years each person had left — the way we can count the years already behind us — how desperately those with only a few years remaining would try to use them well. It's easy to manage any amount carefully when you know exactly how much you have. But the thing you should guard most carefully is something that might run out at any moment — and you never know when.

shortness-of-life_section-08.originalText: Yet you have no reason to suppose that they do not know how dear a thing time is: they are wont to say to those whom they especially love that they are ready to give them a part of their own years. They do give them, and know not that they are giving them; but they give them in such a manner that they themselves lose them without the others gaining them. They do not, however, know whence they obtain their supply, and therefore they are able to endure the waste of what is not seen: yet no one will give you back your years, no one will restore them to you again: your life will run its course when once it has begun, and will neither begin again or efface what it has done.
shortness-of-life_section-08.plainEnglish: You might think people don't understand how precious time is. But they do know. When they love someone deeply, they say they'd give up years of their own life for them. And they actually do give up those years — they just don't realize they're doing it. They give away their time in ways that cost them everything but give the other person nothing. The problem is they don't know where their time comes from, so they can stand to waste what they can't see. But here's the truth: no one will ever give you back those lost years. No one can restore them. Once your life starts moving, it won't stop or start over. It won't undo what's already been done.

shortness-of-life_section-08.originalText: It will make no disturbance, it will give you no warning of how fast it flies: it will move silently on: it will not prolong itself at the command of a king, or at the wish of a nation: as it started on its first day, so it will run: it will never turn aside, never delay. What follows, then? Why! you are busy, but life is hurrying on: death will be here some time or other, and you must attend to him, whether you will or no.
shortness-of-life_section-08.plainEnglish: Time won't make a sound as it passes. It won't warn you how fast it's flying by. It moves in complete silence. No king can order it to slow down. No nation can wish it away. Time runs the same steady pace from your first day to your last. It never turns aside. It never delays. So what does this mean? You're busy with your life, but life is racing past you. Death will arrive someday, and when he does, you'll have to pay attention — whether you want to or not.

shortness-of-life_section-09.originalText: Can anything be mentioned which is more insane than the ideas of leisure of those people who boast of their worldly wisdom? They live laboriously, in order that they may live better; they fit themselves out for life at the expense of life itself, and cast their thoughts a long way forwards: yet postponement is the greatest waste of life: it wrings day after day from us, and takes away the present by promising something hereafter: there is no such obstacle to true living as waiting, which loses to-day while it is depending on the morrow. You dispose of that which is in the hand of Fortune, and you let go that which is in your own. Whither are you looking, whither are you stretching forward? everything future is uncertain: live now straightway.
shortness-of-life_section-09.plainEnglish: Can you think of anything more insane than how these supposedly wise people approach their free time? They work themselves to death so they can live better later. They spend their whole lives preparing to live — but waste their actual life doing it. They're always planning for some distant future. But putting things off is the biggest waste of life there is. It steals day after day from us. It sacrifices the present by promising something better tomorrow. Nothing blocks real living like waiting — losing today while depending on tomorrow. You're betting on what fortune controls, while letting go of what you actually control. Where are you looking? What are you reaching for? Everything in the future is uncertain. Live right now.

shortness-of-life_section-09.originalText: See how the greatest of bards cries to you and sings in wholesome verse as though inspired with celestial fire:— "The best of wretched mortals' days is that Which is the first to fly." Why do you hesitate, says he, why do you stand back? unless you seize it it will have fled: and even if you do seize it, it will still fly. Our swiftness in making use of our time ought therefore to vie with the swiftness of time itself, and we ought to drink of it as we should of a fast-running torrent which will not be always running. The poet, too, admirably satirizes our boundless thoughts, when he says, not "the first age," but "the first day." Why are you careless and slow while time is flying so fast, and why do you spread out before yourself a vision of long months and years, as many as your greediness requires? he talks with you about one day, and that a fast-fleeting one.
shortness-of-life_section-09.plainEnglish: Listen to what the greatest poet tells you. He sings these healthy words as if heaven itself inspired him: 'The best day of our wretched lives is the first one to slip away.' Why do you hesitate? he asks. Why do you hold back? If you don't grab it, it will escape. Even if you do grab it, it will still fly away. So we need to use our time as quickly as time itself moves. We should drink from it like we're drinking from a rushing river that won't flow forever. The poet also brilliantly mocks our endless fantasies. Notice he doesn't say 'the first age' but 'the first day.' Why are you lazy and slow when time flies so fast? Why do you picture long months and years stretching ahead — as many as your greedy heart wants? He's talking to you about one day. And it's racing by.

shortness-of-life_section-09.originalText: There can, then, be no doubt that the best days are those which fly first for wretched, that is, for busy mortals, whose minds are still in their childhood when old age comes upon them, and they reach it unprepared and without arms to combat it. They have never looked forward: they have all of a sudden stumbled upon old age: they never noticed that it was stealing upon them day by day. As conversation, or reading, or deep thought deceives travellers, and they find themselves at their journey's end before they knew that it was drawing near, so in this fast and never-ceasing journey of life, which we make at the same pace whether we are asleep or awake, busy people never notice that they are moving till they are at the end of it.
shortness-of-life_section-09.plainEnglish: There's no doubt about it: the best days slip away first for miserable people — that is, for busy people. Their minds are still childish when old age catches up with them. They reach it unprepared, with no weapons to fight back. They never looked ahead. They stumble into old age all at once. They never noticed it sneaking up on them day by day. Just as conversation, reading, or deep thinking can fool travelers — suddenly they find themselves at their destination before they realized they were getting close — so it is with this fast, never-stopping journey of life. We travel at the same speed whether we're asleep or awake. But busy people never notice they're moving until they reach the end.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: If I chose to divide this proposition into separate steps, supported by evidence, many things occur to me by which I could prove that the lives of busy men are the shortest of all. Fabianus, who was none of your lecture-room philosophers, but one of the true antique pattern, used to say, "We ought to fight against the passions by main force, not by skirmishing, and upset their line of battle by a home charge, not by inflicting trifling wounds: I do not approve of dallying with sophisms; they must be crushed, not merely scratched." Yet, in order that sinners may be confronted with their errors, they must be taught, and not merely mourned for.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: If I wanted to break this argument into steps and back it up with proof, I could show you plenty of evidence that busy people actually live the shortest lives of all. Fabianus wasn't one of those classroom philosophers — he was the real deal, old school. He used to say, "You have to attack your emotions head-on, not dance around them. Charge straight at them and break their ranks. Don't just poke at them with little wounds. I don't believe in playing games with clever arguments — crush them, don't just scratch the surface." But if we want people to see their mistakes, we need to teach them, not just feel sorry for them.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: Life is divided into three parts: that which has been, that which is, and that which is to come: of these three stages, that which we are passing through is brief, that which we are about to pass is uncertain, and that which we have passed is certain: this it is over which Fortune has lost her rights, and which can fall into no other man's power: and this is what busy men lose: for they have no leisure to look back upon the past, and even if they had, they take no pleasure in remembering what they regret: they are, therefore, unwilling to turn their minds to the contemplation of ill-spent time, and they shrink from reviewing a course of action whose faults become glaringly apparent when handled a second time, although they were snatched at when we were under the spell of immediate gratification.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: Life has three parts: the past, the present, and the future. The present moment is brief. The future is uncertain. But the past is secure — it's finished. Fortune can't touch it anymore, and no one can take it away from you. Yet this is exactly what busy people lose. They never take time to look back at their past. And even when they could, they don't enjoy remembering things they regret. So they refuse to think about the time they've wasted. They avoid reviewing their past choices because the mistakes become painfully obvious when you look at them twice — even though those same choices seemed so appealing when we were caught up in the moment.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: No one, unless all his acts have been submitted to the infallible censorship of his own conscience, willingly turns his thoughts back upon the past. He who has ambitiously desired, haughtily scorned, passionately vanquished, treacherously deceived, greedily snatched, or prodigally wasted much, must needs fear his own memory; yet this is a holy and consecrated part of our time, beyond the reach of all human accidents, removed from the dominion of Fortune, and which cannot be disquieted by want, fear, or attacks of sickness: this can neither be troubled nor taken away from one: we possess it for ever undisturbed.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: No one likes to look back on their past unless they can honestly say their conscience is clear. Anyone who has chased success ruthlessly, looked down on others with pride, won through anger, lied to get ahead, grabbed what they could, or thrown away their gifts — they're afraid of their own memories. But here's the thing: the past is actually sacred. It's the one part of our time that nothing can touch. Bad luck can't reach it. Poverty, fear, and disease can't disturb it. No one can trouble it or steal it from you. It's yours forever, completely safe.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: Our present consists only of single days, and those, too, taken one hour at a time: but all the days of past times appear before us when bidden, and allow themselves to be examined and lingered over, albeit busy men cannot find time for so doing. It is the privilege of a tranquil and peaceful mind to review all the parts of its life: but the minds of busy men are like animals under the yoke, and cannot bend aside or look back. Consequently, their life passes away into vacancy, and as you do no good however much you may pour into a vessel which cannot keep or hold what you put there, so also it matters not how much time you give men if it can find no place to settle in, but leaks away through the chinks and holes of their minds.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: Our present is just single days, taken one hour at a time. But all our past days come back when we call them. They let us examine them and spend time with them — if we're not too busy to bother. Only a calm and peaceful mind can review all parts of its life. But the minds of busy people are like animals under a yoke. They can't turn aside or look back. So their life passes away into nothing. Just like pouring water into a broken vessel — it doesn't matter how much you pour in if it can't hold anything. It's the same with time. It doesn't matter how much time you give busy people if it just leaks away through the cracks and holes in their minds.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: Present time is very short, so much so that to some it seems to be no time at all; for it is always in motion, and runs swiftly away: it ceases to exist before it comes, and can no more brook delay than can the universe or the host of heaven, whose unresting movement never lets them pause on their way. Busy men, therefore, possess present time, alone, that being so short that they cannot grasp it, and when they are occupied with many things they lose even this.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: The present moment is very short. So short that some people feel like it doesn't exist at all. It's always moving and rushing away from us. It stops existing before it even arrives, just like the universe and the stars that never pause in their constant movement. Busy people only have this present moment to work with. But it's so brief they can't even grab hold of it. And when they're juggling too many things at once, they lose even this tiny slice of time.

shortness-of-life_section-11.originalText: In a word, do you want to know for how short a time they live? see how they desire to live long: broken-down old men beg in their prayers for the addition of a few more years: they pretend to be younger than they are: they delude themselves with their own lies, and are as willing to cheat themselves as if they could cheat Fate at the same time: when at last some weakness reminds them that they are mortal, they die as it were in terror: they may rather be said to be dragged out of this life than to depart from it. They loudly exclaim that they have been fools and have not lived their lives, and declare that if they only survive this sickness they will spend the rest of their lives at leisure: at such times they reflect how uselessly they have laboured to provide themselves with what they have never enjoyed, and how all their toil has gone for nothing:
shortness-of-life_section-11.plainEnglish: Want to know how short their lives really are? Look at how desperately they want to live longer. Old, broken-down men pray for just a few more years. They lie about their age. They fool themselves with their own lies, willing to deceive themselves as if they could somehow trick Fate too. When illness finally reminds them they're going to die, they're terrified. They don't leave this life — they get dragged out of it kicking and screaming. They cry out that they've been fools, that they never really lived. They promise that if they survive this sickness, they'll finally spend their remaining time on what matters. That's when they realize how pointlessly they worked for things they never enjoyed. All that effort was for nothing.

shortness-of-life_section-11.originalText: but those whose life is spent without any engrossing business may well find it ample: no part of it is made over to others, or scattered here and there; no part is entrusted to Fortune, is lost by neglect, is spent in ostentatious giving, or is useless: all of it is, so to speak, invested at good interest. A very small amount of it, therefore, is abundantly sufficient, and so, when his last day arrives, the wise man will not hang back, but will walk with a steady step to meet death.
shortness-of-life_section-11.plainEnglish: But people who don't waste their lives on meaningless busy work will find they have plenty of time. They don't hand chunks of their life over to other people or scatter it in all directions. They don't leave it up to chance, lose it through carelessness, waste it showing off, or spend it on pointless things. All of it gets invested wisely. So even a small amount of time becomes more than enough. When death finally comes, the wise person won't hesitate or hold back. They'll walk steadily forward to meet it.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Perhaps you will ask me whom I mean by "busy men"? you need not think that I allude only to those who are hunted out of the courts of justice with dogs at the close of the proceedings, those whom you see either honourably jostled by a crowd of their own clients or contemptuously hustled in visits of ceremony by strangers, who call them away from home to hang about their patron's doors, or who make use of the praetor's sales by auction to acquire infamous gains which some day will prove their own ruin. Some men's leisure is busy: in their country house or on their couch, in complete solitude, even though they have retired from all men's society, they still continue to worry themselves: we ought not to say that such men's life is one of leisure, but their very business is sloth.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: You might ask me who I mean by "busy men." Don't think I'm only talking about lawyers who get chased out of courtrooms by bailiffs at closing time. Or those people you see either proudly surrounded by their own clients or rudely pushed around by strangers during formal visits — people who leave home just to wait around at some patron's door, or who use the praetor's auctions to make dirty money that will eventually destroy them. Some people's free time is actually busy. Even in their country house or lying on their couch, completely alone, having withdrawn from everyone — they still find ways to torment themselves. We shouldn't call this kind of life leisurely. Their business is just laziness.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Would you call a man idle who expends anxious finicking care in the arrangement of his Corinthian bronzes, valuable only through the mania of a few connoisseurs? and who passes the greater part of his days among plates of rusty metal? who sits in the palaestra (shame, that our very vices should be foreign) watching boys wrestling? who distributes his gangs of fettered slaves into pairs according to their age and colour? who keeps athletes of the latest fashion?
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: Would you call a man lazy who spends hours fussing over his collection of Corinthian bronze sculptures — valuable only because a few collectors have gone crazy for them? A man who wastes most of his days sorting through piles of rusty metal? Who sits in the gym (how embarrassing that we've even imported our vices from abroad) watching boys wrestle? Who organizes his chained slaves into matching pairs by age and skin color? Who keeps trendy athletes like pets?

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Why, do you call those men idle, who pass many hours at the barber's while the growth of the past night is being plucked out by the roots, holding councils over each several hair, while the scattered locks are arranged in order and those which fall back are forced forward on to the forehead? How angry they become if the shaver is a little careless, as though he were shearing a _man_! what a white heat they work themselves into if some of their mane is cut away, if some part of it is ill-arranged, if all their ringlets do not lie in regular order! who of them would not rather that the state were overthrown than that his hair should be ruffled? who does not care more for the appearance of his head than for his health? who would not prefer ornament to honour?
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: Do you really call these men busy? They spend hours at the barber's getting every hair from last night plucked out by the roots. They hold meetings about each individual hair. They arrange scattered locks just so. They force back hair forward onto their foreheads. Watch how angry they get if the barber slips up a little — as if he were cutting an actual man instead of just hair! See how furious they become if some of their precious mane gets cut too short, or if it's arranged wrong, or if their curls don't lie in perfect order! Which of them wouldn't rather see the government collapse than have his hair messed up? Who doesn't care more about how his head looks than his actual health? Who wouldn't choose a nice hairdo over real honor?

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Do you call these men idle, who make a business of the comb and looking-glass? what of those who devote their lives to composing, hearing, and learning songs, who twist their voices, intended by Nature to sound best and simplest when used straightforwardly, through all the turns of futile melodies: whose fingers are always beating time to some music on which they are inwardly meditating; who, when invited to serious and even sad business may be heard humming an air to themselves?—such people are not at leisure, but are busy about trifles.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: Do you think these people are idle? They spend all their time fussing with their hair and mirrors. What about those who waste their lives writing songs, listening to music, and learning new tunes? They twist their voices through pointless melodies when nature meant voices to sound best when used simply and directly. Their fingers are always tapping out some rhythm they're thinking about. When you invite them to serious business — even sad occasions — you can hear them humming under their breath. These people aren't truly at leisure. They're just busy with worthless things.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: As for their banquets, by Hercules, I cannot reckon them among their unoccupied times when I see with what anxious care they set out their plate, how laboriously they arrange the girdles of their waiters' tunics, how breathlessly they watch to see how the cook dishes up the wild boar, with what speed, when the signal is given, the slave-boys run to perform their duties, how skilfully birds are carved into pieces of the right size, how painstakingly wretched youths wipe up the spittings of drunken men. By these means men seek credit for taste and grandeur, and their vices follow them so far into their privacy that they can neither eat nor drink without a view to effect.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: As for their dinner parties — good God! — I can't call these leisure time when I see how anxiously they arrange their silverware. How carefully they adjust their servants' uniforms. How they hold their breath watching the cook carve the roast boar. How quickly the slave boys sprint to their duties when given a signal. How expertly they slice the birds into perfect portions. How miserably young servants clean up the vomit of drunk guests. Through all this, these hosts are trying to build a reputation for sophistication and luxury. Their need to impress follows them everywhere — they can't even eat or drink without putting on a show.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Nor should I count those men idle who have themselves carried hither and thither in sedans and litters, and who look forward to their regular hour for taking this exercise as though they were not allowed to omit it: men who are reminded by some one else when to bathe, when to swim, when to dine: they actually reach such a pitch of languid effeminacy as not to be able to find out for themselves whether they are hungry.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: I wouldn't call those men idle who get carried around in chairs and litters, who wait for their scheduled exercise time as if they're not allowed to skip it. These are men who need someone else to remind them when to bathe, when to swim, when to eat. They've become so soft and helpless that they can't even tell if they're hungry without someone else's help.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: I have heard one of these luxurious folk—if indeed, we ought to give the name of luxury to unlearning the life and habits of a man—when he was carried in men's arms out of the bath and placed in his chair, say inquiringly, "Am I seated?" Do you suppose that such a man as this, who did not know when he was seated, could know whether he was alive, whether he could see, whether he was at leisure? I can hardly say whether I pity him more if he really did not know or if he pretended not to know this. Such people do really become unconscious of much, but they behave as though they were unconscious of much more: they delight in some failings because they consider them to be proofs of happiness: it seems the part of an utterly low and contemptible man to know what he is doing.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: I once heard one of these pampered rich people—though I'm not sure we should call it luxury when someone forgets how to be human—being carried from his bath to his chair by servants. He asked, "Am I sitting down?" Can you believe that? A man who doesn't know if he's sitting—how could he know if he's truly alive? How could he know if he can see or think clearly? I can't decide what's worse: if he really didn't know, or if he was just pretending not to know. These people genuinely lose awareness of many things. But they also pretend to be unaware of even more. They're actually proud of these failings because they think it proves how wealthy and important they are. Apparently, knowing what you're doing is for common, worthless people.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: After this, do you suppose that playwrights draw largely upon their imaginations in their burlesques upon luxury: by Hercules, they omit more than they invent; in this age, inventive in this alone, such a number of incredible vices have been produced, that already you are able to reproach the playwrights with omitting to notice them. To think that there should be any one who had so far lost his senses through luxury as to take some one else's opinion as to whether he was sitting or not? This man certainly is not at leisure: you must bestow a different title on him: he is sick, or rather dead: he only is at leisure who feels that he is at leisure: but this creature is only half alive, if he wants some one to tell him what position his body is in. How can such a man be able to dispose of any time?
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: After seeing all this, do you think playwrights have to stretch their imaginations when they make fun of luxury? By God, they leave out more than they make up. Our age has gotten so creative with vice that countless unbelievable sins have appeared. Now you could actually criticize playwrights for failing to notice them all. Can you imagine someone so destroyed by luxury that he needs another person to tell him whether he's sitting down or not? This man is definitely not living a life of leisure. You need a different word for him — he's sick, or really he's dead. Only someone who can feel that he's at leisure is truly at leisure. But this poor creature is barely half alive if he needs someone else to tell him what position his body is in. How could such a person possibly control any of his time?

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: It would take long to describe the various individuals who have wasted their lives over playing at draughts, playing at ball, or toasting their bodies in the sun: men are not at leisure if their pleasures partake of the character of business, for no one will doubt that those persons are laborious triflers who devote themselves to the study of futile literary questions, of whom there is already a great number in Rome also. It used to be a peculiarly Greek disease of the mind to investigate how many rowers Ulysses had, whether the Iliad or the Odyssey was written first, and furthermore, whether they were written by the same author, with other matters of the same stamp, which neither please your inner consciousness if you keep them to yourself, nor make you seem more learned, but only more troublesome, if you publish them abroad.
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: It would take too long to list all the people who have wasted their lives playing board games, playing ball, or lying in the sun. These people aren't truly at leisure if their pleasures feel like work. No one would disagree that people who spend their time on pointless academic questions are just busy fools. We already have plenty of these in Rome too. This used to be a uniquely Greek mental illness — debating how many rowers Odysseus had, whether the Iliad or the Odyssey was written first, and whether the same person wrote both. Questions like these don't satisfy you when you think about them privately. And if you share them publicly, they don't make you look smarter — just more annoying.

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: See, already this vain longing to learn what is useless has taken hold of the Romans: the other day I heard somebody telling who was the first Roman general who did this or that: Duillius was the first who won a sea-fight, Curius Dentatus was the first who drove elephants in his triumph: moreover, these stories, though they add nothing to real glory, do nevertheless deal with the great deeds of our countrymen: such knowledge is not profitable, yet it claims our attention as a fascinating kind of folly. I will even pardon those who want to know who first persuaded the Romans to go on board ship. It was Claudius, who for this reason was surnamed Caudex, because any piece of carpentry formed of many planks was called _caudex_ by the ancient Romans, for which reason public records are called _Codices_, and by old custom the ships which ply on the Tiber with provisions are called _codicariae_. Let us also allow that it is to the point to tell how Valerius Corvinus was the first to conquer Messana, and first of the family of the Valerii transferred the name of the captured city to his own, and was called Messana, and how the people gradually corrupted the pronunciation and called him Messalla:
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: Look, this pointless craving to learn useless facts has already infected the Romans. Just the other day I heard someone explaining who was the first Roman general to do this or that: Duillius was the first to win a sea battle, Curius Dentatus was the first to parade elephants in his triumph. These stories don't add anything to real glory, but at least they deal with great deeds by our countrymen. This knowledge isn't useful, yet it grabs our attention like some fascinating foolishness. I'll even forgive people who want to know who first convinced the Romans to get on ships. It was Claudius, who got the nickname Caudex because the ancient Romans called any carpentry made from many planks a 'caudex.' That's why public records are called 'Codices,' and by old tradition the supply ships that work the Tiber are called 'codicariae.' Let's also allow that it's worth mentioning how Valerius Corvinus was the first to conquer Messana, and the first of the Valerius family to transfer the name of the captured city to his own name, and was called Messana — though people gradually corrupted the pronunciation and called him Messalla.

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: or would you let any one find interest in Lucius Sulla having been the first to let lions loose in the circus, they having been previously exhibited in chains, and hurlers of darts having been sent by King Bocchus to kill them? This may be permitted to their curiosity: but can it serve any useful purpose to know that Pompeius was the first to exhibit eighteen elephants in the circus, who were matched in a mimic battle with some convicts? The leading man in the state, and one who, according to tradition, was noted among the ancient leaders of the state for his transcendent goodness of heart, thought it a notable kind of show to kill men in a manner hitherto unheard of. Do they fight to the death? that is not cruel enough: are they torn to pieces? that is not cruel enough: let them be crushed flat by animals of enormous bulk. It would be much better that such a thing should be forgotten, for fear that hereafter some potentate might hear of it and envy its refined barbarity.
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: Would you really want to know that Lucius Sulla was the first to release lions in the circus? Before him, they just kept them chained up. He had dart throwers sent by King Bocchus kill them. Fine, maybe that's interesting trivia. But what good does it do to know that Pompey was the first to put eighteen elephants in the circus and made them fight condemned criminals in a fake battle? Here was the leading man of Rome — someone who was supposedly famous for his kind heart among all the great leaders of the past. And he thought it would be entertaining to kill people in a completely new way. Regular fighting to the death? Not cruel enough. Getting torn apart? Still not cruel enough. Let's have them crushed flat by huge animals! It would be better if we forgot such things completely. Otherwise some future ruler might hear about it and try to copy this sophisticated barbarism.

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: O, how doth excessive prosperity blind our intellects! at the moment at which he was casting so many troops of wretches to be trampled on by outlandish beasts, when he was proclaiming war between such different creatures, when he was shedding so much blood before the eyes of the Roman people, whose blood he himself was soon to shed even more freely, he thought himself the master of the whole world; yet he afterwards, deceived by the treachery of the Alexandrians, had to offer himself to the dagger of the vilest of slaves, and then at last discovered what an empty boast was his surname of "The Great."
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: Oh, how success makes us blind! Pompey was throwing countless prisoners to wild animals. He was staging fights between creatures that should never meet. He was spilling blood in front of the Roman people — the same people whose blood he would soon spill even more freely. At that moment, he thought he ruled the entire world. But later, the Alexandrians tricked him. He had to offer his throat to the knife of the lowest slave. Only then did he realize how empty his nickname "The Great" really was.

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: But to return to the point from which I have digressed, I will prove that even on this very subject some people expend useless pains. The same author tells us that Metellus, when he triumphed after having conquered the Carthaginians in Sicily, was the only Roman who ever had a hundred and twenty captured elephants led before his car: and that Sulla was the last Roman who extended the pomoerium,[7] which it was not the custom of the ancients to extend on account of the conquest of provincial, but only of Italian territory. Is it more useful to know this, than to know that the Mount Aventine, according to him, is outside of the pomoerium, for one of two reasons, either because it was thither that the plebeians seceded, or because when Remus took his auspices on that place the birds which he saw were not propitious: and other stories without number of the like sort, which are either actual falsehoods or much the same as falsehoods? for even if you allow that these authors speak in all good faith, if they pledge themselves for the truth of what they write, still, whose mistakes will be made fewer by such stories? whose passions will be restrained? whom will they make more brave, more just, or more gentlemanly? My friend Fabianus used to say that he was not sure that it was not better not to apply oneself to any studies at all than to become interested in these.
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: But let me get back to my point. I'll show you that people waste their energy even on this kind of learning. The same historian tells us that Metellus was the only Roman who ever paraded 120 captured elephants in his triumph after defeating the Carthaginians in Sicily. He also says that Sulla was the last Roman to extend the pomoerium — something the ancients only did when they conquered Italian territory, not foreign provinces. Is it really more useful to know this than to know why Mount Aventine sits outside the pomoerium? According to him, it's either because the common people retreated there during their rebellion, or because the birds Remus saw there were bad omens. There are countless other stories like this — most of them lies, or close enough to lies. Even if these writers are honest and guarantee what they write is true, who becomes a better person from these stories? Who controls their emotions better? Who becomes braver, more fair, or more decent? My friend Fabianus used to say he wasn't sure it wouldn't be better to skip studying altogether rather than get caught up in this stuff.
