shortness-of-life_section-14.originalText: The only persons who are really at leisure are those who devote themselves to philosophy: and they alone really live: for they do not merely enjoy their own lifetime, but they annex every century to their own: all the years which have passed before them belong to them. Unless we are the most ungrateful creatures in the world, we shall regard these noblest of men, the founders of divine schools of thought, as having been born for us, and having prepared life for us: we are led by the labour of others to behold most beautiful things which have been brought out of darkness into light; we are not shut out from any period, we can make our way into every subject, and, if only we can summon up sufficient strength of mind to overstep the narrow limit of human weakness, we have a vast extent of time wherein to disport ourselves: we may argue with Socrates, doubt with Carneades, repose with Epicurus, overcome human nature with the Stoics, out-herod it with the Cynics. Since Nature allows us to commune with every age, why do we not abstract ourselves from our own petty fleeting span of time, and give ourselves up with our whole mind to what is vast, what is eternal, what we share with better men than ourselves?
shortness-of-life_section-14.plainEnglish: The only people who truly have leisure are those who devote themselves to philosophy. They are the only ones who really live. They don't just enjoy their own lifetime — they add every past century to their own. All the years that came before them belong to them too. Unless we're completely ungrateful, we should see these great thinkers — the founders of divine schools of thought — as having been born for us. They prepared life for us. Through their work, we can see beautiful truths that they brought from darkness into light. We aren't shut out from any time period. We can explore every subject. If we can find the mental strength to go beyond our human limitations, we have a vast amount of time to enjoy ourselves. We can argue with Socrates, question everything with Carneades, find peace with Epicurus, rise above human nature with the Stoics, or reject society with the Cynics. Since nature lets us commune with every age, why do we stay trapped in our own tiny, fleeting moment? Why not give our whole mind to what is vast, eternal, and shared with men better than ourselves?

shortness-of-life_section-14.originalText: Those who gad about in a round of calls, who worry themselves and others, after they have indulged their madness to the full, and crossed every patron's threshold daily, leaving no open door unentered, after they have hawked about their interested greetings in houses of the most various character,—after all, how few people are they able to see out of so vast a city, divided among so many different ruling passions: how many will be moved by sloth, self-indulgence, or rudeness to deny them admittance: how many, after they have long plagued them, will run past them with feigned hurry? how many will avoid coming out through their entrance-hall with its crowds of clients, and will escape by some concealed backdoor? as though it were not ruder to deceive their visitor than to deny him admittance!—how many, half asleep and stupid with yesterday's debauch, can hardly be brought to return the greeting of the wretched man who has broken his own rest in order to wait on that of another, even after his name has been whispered to them for the thousandth time, save by a most offensive yawn of his half-opened lips.
shortness-of-life_section-14.plainEnglish: Think about those people who rush around all day making social calls. They exhaust themselves and everyone else. They go completely crazy with this routine — visiting every powerful person's house each day, never missing an open door. They take their fake, self-serving greetings from house to house, no matter how different these people are. But after all this effort in such a huge city full of people with such different interests, how many do they actually get to see? How many will be too lazy, too indulgent, or too rude to let them in? How many will pretend to be in a hurry and rush right past them after keeping them waiting forever? How many will avoid coming out to their crowded entrance hall and sneak out the back door instead? As if lying to a visitor isn't ruder than just turning him away! And how many are still half-asleep and stupid from last night's drinking? Even after someone whispers the visitor's name to them for the thousandth time, they can barely manage to grunt a greeting back to this poor man who woke up early just to wait around for them. All they can do is yawn with their mouth half-open — and it's insulting.

shortness-of-life_section-14.originalText: We may truly say that those men are pursuing the true path of duty, who wish every day to consort on the most familiar terms with Zeno, Pythagoras, Democritus, and the rest of those high priests of virtue, with Aristotle and with Theophrastus. None of these men will be "engaged," none of these will fail to send you away after visiting him in a happier frame of mind and on better terms with yourself, none of them will let you leave him empty-handed: yet their society may be enjoyed by all men, and by night as well as by day.
shortness-of-life_section-14.plainEnglish: The people on the right track are those who spend time every day with the great thinkers — Zeno, Pythagoras, Democritus, and all the other masters of wisdom, along with Aristotle and Theophrastus. None of these men will be too busy for you. None will send you away feeling worse than when you arrived. They'll always leave you happier and more at peace with yourself. They'll never let you walk away empty-handed. And here's the best part — anyone can enjoy their company, day or night.

shortness-of-life_section-15.originalText: None of these men will force you to die, but all of them will teach you how to die: none of these will waste your time, but will add his own to it. The talk of these men is not dangerous, their friendship will not lead you to the scaffold, their society will not ruin you in expenses: you may take from them whatsoever you will; they will not prevent your taking the deepest draughts of their wisdom that you please. What blessedness, what a fair old age awaits the man who takes these for his patrons! he will have friends with whom he may discuss all matters, great and small, whose advice he may ask daily about himself, from whom he will hear truth without insult, praise without flattery, and according to whose likeness he may model his own character.
shortness-of-life_section-15.plainEnglish: None of these writers will force you to die, but all will teach you how to die well. None will waste your time — they'll add their own time to yours. Their conversation isn't dangerous. Their friendship won't get you executed. Their company won't bankrupt you. You can take whatever you want from them. They won't stop you from drinking deeply from their wisdom. What happiness awaits the person who makes these writers his guides! He'll have friends to discuss everything with, big and small. He can ask their advice about himself every day. He'll hear truth without insults, praise without lies. He can shape his own character to match theirs.

shortness-of-life_section-15.originalText: We are wont to say that we are not able to choose who our parents should be, but that they were assigned to us by chance; yet we may be born just as we please: there are several families of the noblest intellects: choose which you would like to belong to: by your adoption you will not receive their name only, but also their property, which is not intended to be guarded in a mean and miserly spirit: the more persons you divide it among the larger it becomes. These will open to you the path which leads to eternity, and will raise you to a height from whence none shall cast you down. By this means alone can you prolong your mortal life, nay, even turn it into an immortal one.
shortness-of-life_section-15.plainEnglish: People always say we can't choose our parents — that chance assigns them to us. But we can choose to be born into any family we want. There are families of the greatest minds throughout history. Pick which one you'd like to join. When they adopt you, you won't just get their name. You'll inherit their wealth too — and this wealth isn't meant to be hoarded like a miser's gold. The more people you share it with, the more it grows. These great minds will show you the path to eternity. They'll lift you to heights where no one can knock you down. This is the only way to extend your brief life — or even make it immortal.

shortness-of-life_section-15.originalText: High office, monuments, all that ambition records in decrees or piles up in stone, soon passes away: lapse of time casts down and ruins everything; but those things on which Philosophy has set its seal are beyond the reach of injury: no age will discard them or lessen their force, each succeeding century will add somewhat to the respect in which they are held: for we look upon what is near us with jealous eyes, but we admire what is further off with less prejudice. The wise man's life, therefore, includes much: he is not hedged in by the same limits which confine others: he alone is exempt from the laws by which mankind is governed: all ages serve him like a god. If any time be past, he recals it by his memory; if it be present, he uses it; if it be future, he anticipates it: his life is a long one because he concentrates all times into it.
shortness-of-life_section-15.plainEnglish: High office, monuments, all the things that ambition builds up in laws or piles up in stone — they all fade away quickly. Time knocks down and destroys everything. But the things that philosophy has marked as its own can't be harmed. No generation will throw them out or weaken them. Each new century will respect them even more. We look at what's close to us with jealous eyes, but we admire distant things with less bias. So the wise person's life contains much more. He isn't fenced in by the same limits that trap everyone else. He alone is free from the laws that govern humanity. All of history serves him like a god. If some time has passed, he recalls it through memory. If it's present, he uses it. If it's future, he looks forward to it. His life is long because he gathers all times into it.

shortness-of-life_section-16.originalText: Those men lead the shortest and unhappiest lives who forget the past, neglect the present, and dread the future: when they reach the end of it the poor wretches learn too late that they were busied all the while that they were doing nothing. You need not think, because sometimes they call for death, that their lives are long: their folly torments them with vague passions which lead them into the very things of which they are afraid: they often, therefore, wish for death because they live in fear.
shortness-of-life_section-16.plainEnglish: The people who live the shortest and most miserable lives are those who forget their past, ignore their present, and fear their future. When they reach the end, these poor souls realize too late that they stayed busy while accomplishing nothing. Don't think their lives are long just because they sometimes wish for death. Their foolishness torments them with restless desires that drive them toward the very things they fear. So they often wish for death precisely because they live in fear.

shortness-of-life_section-16.originalText: Neither is it, as you might think, a proof of the length of their lives that they often find the days long, that they often complain how slowly the hours pass until the appointed time arrives for dinner: for whenever they are left without their usual business, they fret helplessly in their idleness, and know not how to arrange or to spin it out. They betake themselves, therefore, to some business, and all the intervening time is irksome to them; they would wish, by Hercules, to skip over it, just as they wish to skip over the intervening days before a gladiatorial contest or some other time appointed for a public spectacle or private indulgence: all postponement of what they wish for is grievous to them.
shortness-of-life_section-16.plainEnglish: It's not proof that their lives are long just because they find days boring. They complain about how slowly time drags until dinner arrives. But when they have nothing to do, they panic in their idleness. They don't know how to arrange their time or make it stretch. So they rush to find some activity. All the time in between feels unbearable. By God, they want to skip right over it — just like they want to skip the days before a gladiator fight or some other show they're excited about. Any delay in getting what they want feels terrible to them.

shortness-of-life_section-16.originalText: Yet the very time which they enjoy is brief and soon past, and is made much briefer by their own fault: for they run from one pleasure to another, and are not able to devote themselves consistently to one passion: their days are not long, but odious to them: on the other hand, how short they find the nights which they spend with courtezans or over wine? Hence arises that folly of the poets who encourage the errors of mankind by their myths, and declare that Jupiter to gratify his voluptuous desires doubled the length of the night. Is it not adding fuel to our vices to name the gods as their authors, and to offer our distempers free scope by giving them deity for an example? How can the nights for which men pay so dear fail to appear of the shortest? they lose the day in looking forward to the night, and lose the night through fear of the dawn.
shortness-of-life_section-16.plainEnglish: But even the time these people do enjoy is brief and quickly gone. They make it even shorter through their own mistakes. They jump from one pleasure to another and can't stick with any single passion for long. Their days don't feel long to them — they feel awful. But how short the nights seem when they spend them with prostitutes or drinking! This is where poets get their foolish ideas. They encourage people's mistakes with their stories. They say Jupiter made the night twice as long to satisfy his lustful desires. Isn't this just adding fuel to our vices? When we say the gods are the authors of our bad behavior, we give our diseases free reign by using divinity as our excuse. How can nights that cost men so much fail to seem incredibly short? They waste the day looking forward to night, then waste the night dreading the dawn.

shortness-of-life_section-17.originalText: Such men's very pleasures are restless and disturbed by various alarms, and at the most joyous moment of all there rises the anxious thought: "How long will this last?" This frame of mind has led kings to weep over their power, and they have not been so much delighted at the grandeur of their position, as they have been terrified by the end to which it must some day come. That most arrogant Persian king, when his army stretched over vast plains and could not be counted but only measured, burst into tears at the thought that in less than a hundred years none of all those warriors would be alive; yet their death was brought upon them by the very man who wept over it, who was about to destroy some of them by sea, some on land, some in battle, and some in flight, and who would in a very short space of time put an end to those about whose hundredth year he showed such solicitude. Why need we wonder at their very joys being mixed with fear? they do not rest upon any solid grounds, but are disturbed by the same emptiness from which they spring.
shortness-of-life_section-17.plainEnglish:
Even these people's pleasures are restless and full of worry. Right in the middle of their happiest moments, they think: "How long will this last?" This anxiety has made kings cry about their own power. They weren't celebrating how grand their position was — they were terrified of how it would end.

That arrogant Persian king is a perfect example. His army spread across vast plains. It was so huge you couldn't count it — you could only measure it. But he burst into tears thinking that in less than a hundred years, none of those warriors would still be alive. The irony? He was the one who would kill them. He would destroy some at sea, some on land, some in battle, some while they ran away. In just a short time, he would end the lives of the very men whose future deaths worried him so much.

Why should we be surprised that even their joys are mixed with fear? These pleasures don't rest on solid ground. They're shaken by the same emptiness they come from.

shortness-of-life_section-17.originalText: What must we suppose to be the misery of such times as even they acknowledge to be wretched, when even the joys by which they elevate themselves and raise themselves above their fellows are of a mixed character. All the greatest blessings are enjoyed with fear, and no thing is so untrustworthy as extreme prosperity: we require fresh strokes of good fortune to enable us to keep that which we are enjoying, and even those of our prayers which are answered require fresh prayers. Everything for which we are dependent on chance is uncertain: the higher it rises, the more opportunities it has of falling. Moreover, no one takes any pleasure in what is about to fall into ruin: very wretched, therefore, as well as very short must be the lives of those who work very hard to gain what they must work even harder to keep: they obtain what they wish with infinite labour, and they hold what they have obtained with fear and trembling.
shortness-of-life_section-17.plainEnglish: Think about how miserable these times must be when even the people living them admit they're wretched. Even their greatest joys — the ones that make them feel superior to everyone else — are mixed with anxiety. All our biggest blessings come with fear attached. Nothing is less reliable than extreme success. We need constant new strokes of luck just to keep what we already have. Even when our prayers are answered, we immediately need to pray for more. Everything that depends on chance is uncertain. The higher it climbs, the more ways it can fall. And nobody enjoys something that's about to collapse. So the lives of people who work frantically to get things, then work even harder to keep them, must be both miserable and short. They get what they want through endless struggle. Then they hold onto it in constant fear.

shortness-of-life_section-17.originalText: Meanwhile they take no account of time, of which they will never have a fresh and larger supply: they substitute new occupations for old ones, one hope leads to another, one ambition to another: they do not seek for an end to their wretchedness, but they change its subject. Do our own preferments trouble us? nay, those of other men occupy more of our time. Have we ceased from our labours in canvassing? then we begin others in voting. Have we got rid of the trouble of accusation? then we begin that of judging. Has a man ceased to be a judge? then he becomes an examiner. Has he grown old in the salaried management of other people's property? then he becomes occupied with his own. Marius is discharged from military service; he becomes consul many times: Quintius is eager to reach the end of his dictatorship; he will be called a second time from the plough: Scipio marched against the Carthaginians before he was of years sufficient for so great an undertaking; after he has conquered Hannibal, conquered Antiochus, been the glory of his own consulship and the surety for that of his brother, he might, had he wished it, have been set on the same pedestal with Jupiter; but civil factions will vex the saviour of the state, and he who when a young man disdained to receive divine honours, will take pride as an old man in obstinately remaining in exile. We shall never lack causes of anxiety, either pleasurable or painful: our life will be pushed along from one business to another: leisure will always be wished for, and never enjoyed.
shortness-of-life_section-17.plainEnglish:
Meanwhile, people pay no attention to time — the one thing they can never get more of. They just swap one obsession for another. One hope leads to another hope. One ambition leads to another ambition. They don't try to end their misery. They just change what makes them miserable.

Are you tired of chasing your own promotions? Then you'll spend even more time worrying about other people's promotions. Done campaigning for office? Now you'll campaign for someone else. Finished being the prosecutor? Time to be the judge. Done being a judge? Now you're an investigator. Spent your career managing other people's money? Now you'll obsess over your own.

Look at Marius — discharged from the army, then consul seven times. Quintius couldn't wait to finish his dictatorship, but they'll drag him back from his farm for a second term. Scipio marched against Carthage when he was too young for such a huge task. He beat Hannibal, beat Antiochus, made his consulship famous, and guaranteed his brother's too. He could have been worshipped like a god if he wanted. But political enemies will torment the man who saved the state. The same person who scorned divine honors as a young man will stubbornly cling to exile as an old one.

We'll never run out of things to worry about — pleasant worries or painful ones. Life will push us from one task to the next. We'll always want free time, but we'll never actually enjoy it.

shortness-of-life_section-18.originalText: Whefore, my dearest Paulinus, tear yourself away from the common herd, and since you have seen more rough weather than one would think from your age, betake yourself at length to a more peaceful haven: reflect what waves you have sailed through, what storms you have endured in private life, and brought upon yourself in public. Your courage has been sufficiently displayed by many toilsome and wearisome proofs; try how it will deal with leisure: the greater, certainly the better part of your life, has been given to your country; take now some part of your time for yourself as well. I do not urge you to practise a dull or lazy sloth, or to drown all your fiery spirit in the pleasures which are dear to the herd: that is not rest: you can find greater works than all those which you have hitherto so manfully carried out, upon which you may employ yourself in retirement and security.
shortness-of-life_section-18.plainEnglish: So, my dear Paulinus, pull yourself away from the crowd. You've weathered more storms than someone your age should have. It's time to find a safer harbor. Think about all the waves you've sailed through. Consider the storms you've endured in your private life and the ones you brought on yourself in public service. You've proven your courage through many hard and exhausting trials. Now try using that courage with leisure time. The larger and better part of your life has already been given to your country. Take some of your time for yourself now. I'm not telling you to become dull or lazy, or to drown your fiery spirit in the cheap pleasures that the masses love. That's not real rest. You can find greater works than all the ones you've so bravely accomplished — works you can pursue in retirement and safety.

shortness-of-life_section-18.originalText: You manage the revenues of the entire world, as unselfishly as though they belonged to another, as laboriously as if they were your own, as scrupulously as though they belonged to the public: you win love in an office in which it is hard to avoid incurring hatred; yet, believe me, it is better to understand your own mind than to understand the corn-market. Take away that keen intellect of yours, so well capable of grappling with the greatest subjects, from a post which may be dignified, but which is hardly fitted to render life happy, and reflect that you did not study from childhood all the branches of a liberal education merely in order that many thousand tons of corn might safely be entrusted to your charge: you have given us promise of something greater and nobler than this. There will never be any want of strict economists or of laborious workers: slow-going beasts of burden are better suited for carrying loads than well-bred horses, whose generous swiftness no one would encumber with a heavy pack.
shortness-of-life_section-18.plainEnglish: You manage the world's finances as unselfishly as if the money belonged to someone else. You work as hard as if it were your own money. You're as careful as if it were public funds. You've won people's love in a job where most people end up hated. But believe me — it's better to understand your own mind than to understand the grain market. Take that sharp mind of yours away from this job. Yes, it's a respectable position, but it won't make you happy. Remember, you didn't spend your childhood studying everything just so you could manage thousands of tons of grain. You promised us something greater and nobler than this. There will always be plenty of careful accountants and hard workers. Slow pack animals are better for carrying heavy loads than thoroughbred horses — no one would weigh down a racehorse with a heavy pack.

shortness-of-life_section-18.originalText: Think, moreover, how full of risk is the great task which you have undertaken: you have to deal with the human stomach: a hungry people will not endure reason, will not be appeased by justice, and will not hearken to any prayers. Only just a few days ago, when G. Caesar perished, grieving for nothing so much (if those in the other world can feel grief) as that the Roman people did not die with him, there was said to be only enough corn for seven or eight days' consumption: while he was making bridges with ships and playing with the resources of the empire, want of provisions, the worst evil that can befall even a besieged city, was at hand: his imitation of a crazy outlandish and misproud king very nearly ended in ruin, famine, and the general revolution which follows famine. What must then have been the feelings of those who had the charge of supplying the city with corn, who were in danger of stoning, of fire and sword, of Gaius himself? With consummate art they concealed the vast internal evil by which the state was menaced, and were quite right in so doing; for some diseases must be cured without the patient's knowledge: many have died through discovering what was the matter with them.
shortness-of-life_section-18.plainEnglish: Think about how risky your job really is. You have to deal with the human stomach. Hungry people won't listen to reason. They won't be satisfied by justice. They won't hear your prayers. Just a few days ago, when Caligula died — mourning nothing more (if the dead can mourn) than that the Roman people didn't die with him — there was only enough grain left for seven or eight days. While he was building bridges out of ships and playing games with the empire's resources, we were facing starvation. That's the worst thing that can happen even to a city under siege. His copying of some crazy foreign king almost ended in disaster, famine, and the revolution that always follows famine. What must the grain officials have felt? They faced stoning, fire, sword — even Caligus himself. They hid this massive internal threat to the state with great skill. And they were right to do it. Some diseases must be treated without the patient knowing. Many people have died just from learning what was wrong with them.

shortness-of-life_section-19.originalText:
Betake yourself to these quieter, safer, larger fields of
action: do you think that there can be any comparison between seeing
that corn is deposited in the public granary without being
stolen by the fraud or spoilt by the carelessness of the importer,
that it does not suffer from damp or overheating, and that it
measures and weighs as much as it ought, and beginning the study
of sacred and divine knowledge, which will teach you of what elements
the gods are formed, what are their pleasures, their position, their
form? to what changes your soul has to look forward? where Nature
will place us when we are dismissed from our bodies? what that
principle is which holds all the heaviest particles of our universe
in the middle, suspends the lighter ones above, puts fire highest
of all, and causes the stars to rise in their courses, with many
other matters, full of marvels? Will you not[10] cease to grovel
on earth and turn your mind’s eye on these themes? nay, while your
blood still flows swiftly, before your knees grow feeble, you ought
to take the better path. In this course of life there await you
many good things, such as love and practice of the virtues,
forgetfulness of passions, knowledge of how to live and die, deep
repose. The position of all busy men is unhappy, but most unhappy
of all is that of those who do not even labour at their own affairs,
but have to regulate their rest by another man’s sleep, their walk
by another man’s pace, and whose very love and hate, the freest
things in the world, are at another’s bidding. If such men wish to
know how short their lives are, let them think how small a fraction
of them is their own.
shortness-of-life_section-19.plainEnglish: Turn to these quieter, safer, more important activities. Do you really think there's any comparison between checking that grain gets stored in public warehouses without being stolen or ruined by careless importers — making sure it doesn't get damp or overheated, and that it weighs what it should — and beginning to study sacred and divine knowledge? This study will teach you what the gods are made of, what gives them pleasure, where they live, what they look like. It will show you what changes your soul can expect, where Nature will place us when we leave our bodies, what force holds the heaviest parts of our universe in the center and suspends the lighter ones above, puts fire at the top, and makes the stars move in their courses — along with many other wonderful mysteries. Won't you stop crawling around on earth and turn your mind's eye to these topics? While your blood still flows quickly and before your knees grow weak, you should take the better path. On this road, many good things wait for you: love and practice of virtue, freedom from destructive emotions, knowledge of how to live and die, deep peace. The situation of all busy people is miserable. But most miserable of all are those who don't even work on their own affairs. They have to time their rest by someone else's sleep, their walks by someone else's pace. Even their love and hate — the freest things in the world — are controlled by others. If such people want to know how short their lives are, let them think about how small a fraction of their time is actually their own.

shortness-of-life_section-20.originalText: When, therefore, you see a man often wear the purple robes of office, and hear his name often repeated in the forum, do not envy him: he gains these things by losing so much of his life. Men throw away all their years in order to have one year named after them as consul: some lose their lives during the early part of the struggle, and never reach the height to which they aspired: some after having submitted to a thousand indignities in order to reach the crowning dignity, have the miserable reflexion that the only result of their labours will be the inscription on their tombstone.
shortness-of-life_section-20.plainEnglish: So when you see a man wearing the purple robes of high office, and when you hear his name repeated constantly in the forum, don't envy him. He bought those things by throwing away years of his life. Men waste entire lifetimes just to have one year named after them as consul. Some die during the early struggle and never reach the heights they dreamed of. Others endure a thousand humiliations to reach that final honor, only to realize with misery that all their work will amount to nothing more than words carved on their tombstone.

shortness-of-life_section-20.originalText: Some, while telling off extreme old age, like youth, for new aspirations, have found it fail from sheer weakness amid great and presumptuous enterprises. It is a shameful ending, when a man's breath deserts him in a court of justice, while, although well stricken in years, he is still striving to gain the sympathies of an ignorant audience for some obscure litigant: it is base to perish in the midst of one's business, wearied with living sooner than with working; shameful, too, to die in the act of receiving payments, amid the laughter of one's long-expectant heir.
shortness-of-life_section-20.plainEnglish: Some people scold extreme old age for having the same foolish ambitions as youth. But then they collapse from weakness while chasing big, arrogant projects. What a shameful way to end — when your breath gives out in a courtroom while you're still trying to win over some ignorant crowd for some nobody client. How pathetic to die in the middle of your business dealings, worn out by life before you're worn out by work. And how embarrassing to drop dead while collecting money, with your heir laughing in the background after waiting so long for you to finally go.

shortness-of-life_section-20.originalText: I cannot pass over an an instance which occurs to me: Turannius was an old man of the most painstaking exactitude, who after entering upon his ninetieth year, when he had by G. Caesar's own act been relieved of his duties as collector of the revenue, ordered himself to be laid out on his bed and mourned for as though he were dead. The whole house mourned for the leisure of its old master, and did not lay aside its mourning until his work was restored to him. Can men find such pleasure in dying in harness? Yet many are of the same mind: they retain their wish for labour longer than their capacity for it, and fight against their bodily weakness; they think old age an evil for no other reason than because it lays them on the shelf.
shortness-of-life_section-20.plainEnglish: I can't skip this story that comes to mind: Turannius was an extremely careful old man who had worked as a tax collector. When he turned ninety, Emperor Caius Caesar officially retired him from his job. So what did Turannius do? He had himself laid out on his bed like a corpse and mourned as if he were dead. His entire household mourned their old master's retirement. They didn't stop mourning until he got his job back. Can you believe it? Some people actually find joy in working themselves to death. Many others think the same way. They want to keep working long after their bodies can handle it. They fight against their physical weakness. They think old age is terrible for one reason only — because it forces them to stop working.

shortness-of-life_section-20.originalText: The law does not enrol a soldier after his fiftieth year, or require a senator's attendance after his sixtieth: but men have more difficulty in obtaining their own consent than that of the law to a life of leisure. Meanwhile, while they are plundering and being plundered, while one is disturbing another's repose, and all are being made wretched alike, life remains without profit, without pleasure, without any intellectual progress: no one keeps death well before his eyes, no one refrains from far-reaching hopes. Some even arrange things which lie beyond their own lives, such as huge sepulchral buildings, the dedication of public works, and exhibitions to be given at their funeral-pyre, and ostentatious processions: but, by Hercules, the funerals of such men ought to be conducted by the light of torches and wax tapers, as though they had lived but a few days.
shortness-of-life_section-20.plainEnglish: The law won't make a soldier serve past fifty or require a senator to show up past sixty. But people have a harder time giving themselves permission to rest than getting legal permission. Meanwhile, they keep stealing from each other and getting robbed in return. They disturb each other's peace and make everyone miserable. Life becomes pointless — no profit, no pleasure, no growth. No one remembers they're going to die. No one stops making grand plans for the distant future. Some even plan things that will happen after they're dead: massive tombs, public monuments, elaborate funeral games, and showy processions. But honestly, these people's funerals should be held with just a few torches and candles — as if they had only lived a few days.
